prompt.context: Your client is a successful entrepreneur based in Manhattan. She is always thinking of creative ways to start new businesses. Her latest idea is to build a floating hotel (think of a skyscraper on a barge, and the combined structure is seaworthy). Today is Oct. 1, and she must make a decision ASAP — her preferred construction company and barge manufacturer conveniently have openings on Nov. 1 for projects. If she misses this window it will be another two years before both companies can simultaneously work together. The entrepreneur hires you to assess whether she should spend $20M to build a floating hotel that is seaworthy.
prompt.question: Should the client spend $20M to build a seaworthy floating hotel? Specifically, can the project meet a 20% ROI in the first year of operation?

clarifying_info.q: Can the hotel actually travel on water?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the hotel can travel on water like a sea vessel.

clarifying_info.q: How long does construction and validation take?
Where will the hotel be built?
clarifying_info.a: The hotel and barge will be fabricated in New Jersey.
Two-city strategy: Miami from Nov. 1 to Apr. 30, and Manhattan from May 1 to Oct. 31, to take advantage of high seasons year-round.
The $20M is a sunk investment representing all labor, material, and testing costs to manufacture and validate the seaworthy floating hotel.
20% ROI in the first year of operation.

clarifying_info.q: When does the client want to start operating?
clarifying_info.a: She wants to begin operating as soon as construction and testing conclude — Nov. 1 of the following year.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client have enough money?
clarifying_info.a: Assume the client has sufficient funds.

framework: Financial Analysis: Initial investment ($20M sunk), Revenue (rooms, first-floor amenities), Costs (variable and fixed per city), ROI vs. 20% target
Market Analysis: Travel & tourism industry growth, competitive landscape (no other seaworthy floating hotels in US), substitutes (chain hotels, B&Bs, RVs, weekly rentals), market size unknown

Implementation Considerations: Location strategy (Miami/Manhattan two-city), size and capacity, competition and barriers to entry, marketing strategy and target segments, safety (tropical storms/hurricanes), management and hospitality expertise, regulatory/licensing compliance

questions.prompt: Conduct a market analysis: what is the competitive landscape and what locations should the client consider?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note the Travel & Tourism industry has good growth in tourist cities. There are no other seaworthy floating hotels in the US (East or West Coast), giving the client a first-mover advantage. Other competitors and substitutes are numerous and fragmented (chain hotels, motels, B&Bs, campers/RVs, weekly apartment rentals). The exact industry size and market share are unknown. The client is only considering the US East Coast. Government regulations will be addressed during construction and validation phases. Candidate should then reason toward a two-city strategy (Miami in winter high season, Manhattan in summer high season).

questions.prompt: Calculate total annual revenue for the hotel.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify two revenue streams: (1) room revenue across floors 2-26, and (2) first-floor amenity revenue (restaurant, bar/discotheque, convenience shop). Key data to elicit: 26 floors total, floors 2-26 have rooms (25 floors), each floor is a 5x5 grid = 25 rooms/floor, 80% occupancy year-round, $200/room/night room rate, first-floor aggregate revenue = $200,000/month.

math.setup: First Floor Revenue = $200,000/month x 12 months. Room Revenue = Rooms/floor x Floors with rooms x Occupancy x Rate x Days/year.
steps: Annual Room Revenue = 25 rooms/floor x 25 floors x 0.80 x $200/night x 360 days = $36,000,000/year

questions.prompt: Identify and calculate total annual costs, split by variable and fixed costs for each city.
questions.guidance: Variable costs include housekeeping and food & drink. Fixed costs include docking fees (significant), insurance (massive), and yearly regulatory fees. A key nuance: federal regulations mandate internal and external housekeeping regardless of occupancy, so VC applies to all 625 rooms every day of the season. Costs differ by city. Miami: VC = $100/room/day, FC = $1M/season (180 days). Manhattan: VC = $150/room/day, FC = $3M/season (180 days). Seasonality does not affect VC or FC rates.

math.setup: Total rooms = 25 floors x 25 rooms = 625 rooms. Each city operates 180 days. VC applies to all rooms every day regardless of occupancy.

questions.prompt: Calculate the ROI and determine whether the client meets her 20% target.
questions.guidance: ROI = Profit / Investment x 100%. Profit = Total Revenue - Total Cost. Investment = $20M sunk cost. Candidate should clearly state whether the result exceeds the 20% target.

steps: Client target = 20% ROI; Resulting ROI ≈ 31.4% — target exceeded

brainstorming.prompt: What risks should the client be aware of, and what mitigating factors exist?

categories.name: Demand / Occupancy Risk
ideas: Risk of being first to market and not achieving the anticipated 80% occupancy rate
Mitigate with promotions and advance sales to secure early bookings; since ROI > objective, the client can trim the top line and still meet the financial target

categories.name: Competitive Risk
ideas: Strong profits will attract competitors, who may enter the market
Increased competition could drive up docking fees and upset the profit equation
Secure multi-year contracts for docking in Miami and Manhattan while first-mover advantage exists

categories.name: Regulatory / Safety Risk
ideas: Hotel must be built to withstand tropical storms and hurricanes in Miami
Government regulations must be fully addressed during construction and validation phases

categories.name: Operational Risk
ideas: Management must have dual expertise: hospitality and maritime operations
External housekeeping (daily exterior inspections) is federally mandated regardless of occupancy, adding to VC

recommendation: The client should proceed with construction on Nov. 1 to fabricate a seaworthy floating hotel
The project yields an ROI of approximately 31%, surpassing the 20% financial objective
The hotel's unique ability to operate as a sea vessel enables it to capitalise on high tourism seasons in both Miami (winter) and Manhattan (summer)
The client has adequate funding to finance the project
risks: Failing to achieve the anticipated 80% occupancy rate as a first-of-its-kind concept
Competitors entering the market once strong profits are visible, potentially driving up docking fees
Exposure to severe weather events (hurricanes/tropical storms) in the Miami operating season
next_steps: Ensure contracts are drawn up with both the hotel and barge manufacturers before Nov. 1
Scout and secure port locations in Manhattan and Miami
Negotiate and sign multi-year docking fee contracts in both cities to lock in costs before competitors arrive
Begin advertising campaign at least 6 months in advance of the hotel's Nov. 1 opening
